To recuse means to remove yourself from a decision, a case, or a process because you have a personal interest or bias in the outcome — or because a reasonable person looking at the situation from the outside would think you might be biased, even if you believe you aren't.

The most important thing to understand right away: recusing is about stepping aside completely. It doesn't mean "trying harder to be fair." It means removing yourself from the matter entirely — no voting, no judging, no deciding, no participating.

Imagine a judge is assigned to a case. Now imagine that one of the two parties in the case is the judge's own brother. Even if the judge sincerely believes she can be completely fair and impartial, the situation looks compromised. Other people would rightfully ask: "Can we really trust a ruling made by someone whose own brother stands to benefit?"

So the judge recuses herself — she formally steps away from the case, and a different judge takes over. That is recusal.
The Key Trigger: Conflict of Interest

You recuse yourself when you have what's called a conflict of interest. This means your personal situation — your relationships, your financial holdings, your past work, your personal beliefs about a specific matter — creates a situation where you cannot be, or cannot appear to be, a neutral decision-maker.

Common triggers for recusal include:

  • Financial interest — A judge owns stock in a company that is a party in the case before them.
  • Personal relationships — A board member is asked to evaluate a contract with a company run by their spouse.
  • Prior involvement — A government official is asked to rule on a policy at their former employer.
  • Personal bias — A juror has publicly stated strong opinions about the defendant before the trial.

In every one of these situations, the right move is to recuse — to say, "I should not be the one making this call."

Recusal can happen in two ways:

1. You recuse yourself (voluntary).
This is by far the most common and most respected form. You recognize the conflict, you declare it openly, and you step aside on your own. This is usually expressed as "recuse oneself" — as in, "The senator recused himself from the vote."

2. You are recused by others (forced/ordered).
Sometimes a person fails to recognize — or refuses to acknowledge — their own conflict of interest. In that case, the court, an ethics board, or another governing body can formally remove them from the matter. This is expressed passively — "The official was recused from the investigation."
Where You'll See This Word Used

While recusal is most famously associated with judges and courts, it is used across many formal settings:

  • Politics: A lawmaker recuses themselves from a vote on legislation that would directly benefit their family's business.
  • Corporate boards: A board member recuses themselves from a discussion about acquiring a company they have an ownership stake in.
  • Government agencies: A regulator recuses themselves from overseeing an industry they previously worked in.
  • Academic panels: A professor recuses themselves from grading a student they have a close personal relationship with.
  • Arbitration and mediation: A neutral third-party arbitrator recuses themselves after it's discovered they previously worked for one of the disputing sides.
An Important Nuance: Appearance Is Enough

Here is a subtle but critical point that many learners miss: you don't have to actually be biased to need to recuse yourself. The mere appearance of a conflict is sufficient.

The law and ethics broadly recognize that public trust in fair processes depends not just on decisions being fair, but on them looking fair to ordinary people. If a reasonable, neutral person looking at your situation would think, "Hmm, this person probably has a personal stake in the outcome," that is enough to require recusal — even if you could, in practice, make a perfectly fair decision.

This principle is sometimes stated as: "Justice must not only be done, it must be seen to be done."

Most common construction — reflexive:

  • "The judge recused herself from the case."
  • "He recused himself from all matters involving his former employer."

Passive construction:

  • "The official was recused from the investigation."
  • "She was asked to be recused from the vote."

As a gerund/noun phrase:

  • "His recusing himself from the hearing was widely praised."

Related word forms to know:

  • Recusal (noun): the act of recusing — "The senator announced her recusal from the committee vote."
  • Recused (past tense / past participle): "The judge was recused."
  • Recusing (present participle): "She is recusing herself from all pending cases."
How It Differs From Simply "Withdrawing" or "Stepping Down"

These are related but not the same:

  • To withdraw from something just means to remove yourself, for any reason at all (you're too busy, you changed your mind, etc.). There's no implication of a conflict.
  • To step down usually means resigning from a role or position entirely and permanently.
  • To recuse is specifically about temporarily and formally stepping aside from a particular matter because of a specific conflict of interest — you're not necessarily leaving your role altogether. The judge who recuses from one case still presides over all their other cases. The senator who recuses from one vote still participates in all others.

To recuse is to formally remove yourself (or be removed) from involvement in a specific decision or process because your personal circumstances create — or appear to create — a conflict of interest that could compromise your impartiality.
